titleStmt.title: Simultaneous Progressing Switching Protocols for Timing Predictable Real-Time Network-on-Chips

analytic.title: Simultaneous Progressing Switching Protocols for Timing Predictable Real-Time Network-on-Chips

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Inter-core communication is a central challenge in many-core systems for which Network-on-chips (NoCs) have been demonstrated to scale well and to provide good overall performance. However, not only the distributed structure but also the link switching of NoCs have imposed a great challenge in the design and analysis for real-time systems where timing verification is mandatory. NoC protocols like worm-hole switching are designed with scalability and flexibility in mind, thus the existing link switching protocols usually consider each single link to be scheduled independently. The flexibility of such linkbased arbitrations allows each packet to be distributed over multiple switches but also increases the number of possible link states (the number of flits in a buffer) that have to be considered in the worst-case timing analysis for real-time systems. To achieve timing predictability by design, we propose a family of less flexible switching protocols, called Simultaneous Progressing Switching Protocols (SP 2 ), in which the links used by a flow either all simultaneously transmit one flit (if it exists) of this flow or none of them transmits any flit of this flow. Based on the all-or-nothing property of SP 2 , we reduce the schedulability of the NoC to the uniprocessor self-suspension scheduling problem. Moreover, the proposed approach is not limited to any specific underlying routing protocols, which are usually constructed for deadlock avoidance instead of timing predictability.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Power dissipation has constrained the performance scaling of single-core systems in the past decade. Hence, instead of increasing the operational frequency of a processor, chip manufacturers have shifted their design focus towards chips with multiple or many cores that operate at lower voltages and frequencies than their single-core counterparts. In a multi-or many-core system, communication and synchronization of the applications executed on different cores have to be designed efficiently from both hardware and software perspectives.

The communication fabric of a multi-or many-core platform must scale with the number of cores. Otherwise, the computation capacity of the cores may be wasted if they are waiting for communication, synchronization, or memory access. One possible approach to achieve good scalability of communications is the Network-on-Chip (NoC) architecture, in which a switched network with switches is used to provide the interconnection of the physical cores on a chip. The NoC architecture allows parallel inter-core communication with moderate hardware costs. NoCs are the prevalent choice of interconnection due to their overall good performance and scalability potential as reported by Kavaldjiev et. al [16].

The efficiency of a NoC depends on many design factors, including topology, routing protocols, flow control, switching arbitration protocols, etc. The currently available multi-core platforms based on NoCs have employed different topologies, e.g., a ring in the Intel Xeon Phi 3120A, a 2-D torus in MPPA Manycores by Kalray, and a 2-D mesh in Tilera TILE-Gx8036. Moreover, many different communication protocols and communication topologies have been proposed and evaluated in the literature. Specifically, flit-based NoCs have been proposed with the goal to decrease production cost and increase energy efficiency due to less complex switches and decreased buffer sizes compared to other approaches.

Many safety-critical embedded systems must comply with real-time constraints, e.g., timing-sensitive applications in embedded mobile platforms, automotive, and aerospace applications. Such real-time systems must be constructed with formal verification of timeliness constraints in mind. To construct a hard real-time system on a NoC, each hard real-time message (defined as an instance of a sporadic/periodic flow) in the NoC has to be successfully transmitted from its source to its destination before its deadline.

Approaches for real-time communication on a NoC apply one of two general strategies. One is to utilize time-divisionmultiplexing (TDM) to ensure that the timing constraints are satisfied by constructing the transmission schedule statically with a repetitive table, e.g., in [8], [9], [13], [20], [25], [28], [29], [31]. Another is to apply a priority-based dynamic scheduling strategy in the switches (and switches) to arbitrate the flits in the network, e.g., in [10]- [12], [14], [15], [17], [19], [21]- [23], [30], [34], [35]. The difficulty of the TDM strategy is to construct a feasible TDM schedule and the global clock synchronization, whilst the difficulty of the prioritybased scheduling strategy is to validate the schedulability, i.e., whether all messages can meet their deadlines.

With respect to fixed-priority based scheduling strategies, Table VII in [11] summarizes the recent results for fixedpriority worm-hole switched NoCs up to 2017. Eight of the ten results (namely, [10], [11], [14], [15], [17], [19], [21], [23], [30], [34]) were already disproved by counter examples. These flaws in the literature potentially suggest that the scheduling algorithm and network architecture may be too complex to be correctly analyzed adopting uniprocessor real-time scheduling theory. In the position papers concerning the design of predictable systems by Wilhelm et al. [33] and Axer et. al [2], the authors state that system properties that are subject to predictability constraints should already be considered and guaranteed from the design. Furthermore, the authors note that since the overall timing requirements of the system are propagated down in the system hierarchy, all parts of the system must be designed with respect to predictability. Following this position, we focus on the design of a protocol that allows for simple worst-case transmission latency and backpressure analyses by design. Moreover, we show how to reduce the schedulability problem to existing uniprocessor scheduling theory.

Contributions: In this paper, we revisit the fundamental problem of NoC arbitration protocols with respect to real-time constraints. In addition, we identify the analytic pessimism of worm-hole switched fixed-priority arbitration protocols due to the large degree of uncertainty in the system behaviour which results in hardly verifiable timeliness properties. This paper intends to answer two unsolved fundamental questions for real-time NoCs and has the following contributions:

• What is the fundamental difficulty of worst-case timing analysis using scheduling theory when flit-based transmissions are handled by switch-based (link-based) scheduling? We show that the difficulty is mainly due to the explosion of the possible progression states of a message in the transmission path. Moreover, we argue why priority-based scheduling without controlling the number of possible progression states is therefore difficult to be analyzed and optimized. The existing analyses did not focus on proving the coverage of all possible progression states. • Is it possible to formally prove the equivalence of uniprocessor scheduling and NoC switching so that the rich literature of timing analysis in uniprocessor real-time systems can be applied? To the best of our knowledge, such an equivalence has not been shown for any flit-based NoC arbitration protocols, like worm-hole switching. In this paper, we show that the equivalence can be achieved for less flexible switching protocols. Towards this, we propose a family of SP 2 , in which the links used by a message either all simultaneously transmit one flit of this message or none of them transmits any flit of this message. Such an all-or-nothing property of the SP 2 relates the scheduling behavior on the network to the uniprocessor self-suspension scheduling problem. We provide rigorous proofs to confirm the equivalence of these two problems. • Regarding the implementation of SP 2 , it is important to identify which flows can be transmitted at a specific time point without collision. We sketch how to implement SP 2 based on centralized arbitration.

Preemptive worm-hole switching with virtual channels is designed for a good average-case performance. The complex progression states and complex congestion patterns due to backpressure are a source of complications for timing analyses. We believe that our conceptual proposals can be a beneficial first step towards the design and analysis of timing-predictable switching protocols of NoCs that allow for easier timingand backpressure analysis, and arbitrary deadlock-free routing schemes.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: For dynamic scheduling strategies, the worm-hole switched fixed-priority NoC with preemptive virtual channels has been considered. The first attempts to tackle the schedulability analysis were in 1994 in [21] and 1997 in [10]. Both of them were found to be flawed in 1998 by Kim et al. [17], whose analysis was later found to be erroneous in 2005 by Lu et al. [19]. The series of erroneous analyses continued in [10], [17], [19], [21]. Shi and Burns [30] published an analysis in 2008. Eight years later, Xiong et al. [34] pointed out that the analyses in [30] are unsafe in the sense that they do not consider limited buffer space and virtual channels. The proposed analysis by Xiong et al. [34] was later disproved by counter examples and fixed by the authors in their journal revision in [35] in 2017. In addition, Kashif et al. [14] proposed stage-level analysis (SLA) to improve the analysis by Shi and Burns in [30]. The SLA in [14] assumes an infinite buffer size. Kashif and Patel [15] extended the SLA analysis to cope with limited buffer size, which was disproved by Xiong et al. [34].

In the mean time, Indrusiak et al. [11], [12] presented new analyses, but they "chose to provide intuitions, insight and experimental evidence on the proposed analysis and its improvements, rather than theorems or proofs." They supported their analyses by evaluating concrete cases, i.e., whether there was any observed case which was claimed to meet the deadlines but in fact missed the deadlines. However, such case studies cannot validate the correctness of their analyses, as also stated by Indrusiak et al. [11], [12].

Irrespective of the model assumptions, all described analyses that use real-time scheduling theory to obtain worst-case end-to-end response times assume uniprocessor equivalence and base their proofs on this assumption, i.e., using the critical instant theorem without considering the mismatch between the uniprocessor scheduling model and the worm-hole switching.

Avoiding the obstacle of timing analysis discussed above, in 2019, Nikolíc et al. [22] proposed a slot-based transmission protocol, which applies two parallel domains, one for arbitration and one for data transmission.

The worst-case response time of worm-hole switched fixedpriority NoCs with preemptive virtual channels can also be determined by applying Network Calculus and Compositional Performance Analysis (CPA), or their extensions, to analyze the transmission on the links in a compositional manner, e.g., [1], [3], [4], [26], [27], [32]. Giroudot and Mifdaoui [7] use network-calculus to derive worst-case end-to-end response times for worm-hole switched fixed-priority NoCs with limited virtual channels and limited buffer space. In contrast to their work, we intend to design a NoC switching protocol that yields predictable (uniprocessor equivalent) congestion patterns even for a limited number of buffers and virtual channels as well as arbitrary deadlock-free routing ability.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL AND PROBLEM DEFINITION
div.p: Network-on-Chips (NoCs) are characterized by the topology, routing protocol, arbitration, buffering, flow control mechanism, and switching protocol. 1 In this paper, we define a NoC as a collection of cores A, switches V, and links Λ. Each switch is connected to at least one other switch by two physically separate links, i.e., up-link and down-link. We assume that all the cores, switches, and links are homogeneous. Therefore, the transmission rate and processing capability are identical.

With respect to switching, three different switching protocols have been established, namely, circuit switching, storeand-forward switching, and worm-hole switching. Circuit Switching: A packet (transmission unit) is forwarded by the switches through dedicated routes that are reserved/allocated until the transmission is finished. Therefore, each transmission can only be preempted during the establishing of a route. An advantage of this approach is that no buffers are required and subsequent deadlock-free routing, which allows for optimized and adaptive routing schemes. However, the overhead to establish the routes may render this approach infeasible when small packets are injected frequently. Store-And-Forward Switching: switches can only forward a packet once it is completely received and stored, which implies that the switches must provide sufficient buffer capacity to store a complete packet. Fortunately, the arbitration protocol is suitable for real-time analysis, since a packet may compete for at most one link at each point in time. It is, however, not useful in practice because of the large buffer requirement. Wormhole-Switching: Each packet is divided into smaller transmission units, called flits, always including a designated header and a designated tail flit which are used for control and routing. That is, each payload flit follows the output port of the header flit. In fixed-priority worm-hole switched NoCs, each switch contains virtual channels, i.e., separated buffers that contain flits of a single packet. Once the tail flit is transmitted and removed from the buffer, the virtual channel can be used for flits of another packet. Furthermore, the highest-priority flit is scheduled to transmit over the link at each switch. In this approach, complete packets do not have to be buffered, which allows smaller buffers in the hardware design. On the downside, each packet may be distributed over multiple switches and subsequently compete for multiple links at the same time which makes the timing analysis complex. Additionally, the limited number of virtual channels and full buffers on the receiving switch add additional interference which complicates the analysis. 1 Our notation of flows is equivalent to tasks and our notation of messages is equivalent to jobs in the classical notation of the real-time systems community.

div.head: A. Messages and Periodic/Sporadic Flows
div.p: A periodic (sporadic) flow f i generates an infinite sequence of flow instances, called messages, with following parameters:

• T i is the minimum inter-arrival time or period of the flow f i , i.e., for a periodic flow one message is released exactly every T i time units and for a sporadic flow two subsequent messages are separated by at least T i . • Λ i is an arbitrary static routing path of the flow f i , i.e., λ i1 , λ i2 , . . . , λ iηi is the sequence of the η i links that a message of f i has to be transmitted on. We assume that a physical link cannot be used more than once in the static routing path Λ i for any i. • C i is the largest number of flits (worst-case) of a message of f i . • D i is the relative deadline of the flow f i . That is, when a message is injected at time t, its absolute deadline is t + D i , at which the last flit of the message has to reach the destination. Our protocols are not restricted to any specific relation of the minimum inter-arrival time and the relative deadline D i , but our timing analysis focuses on constrained-deadline flows, where D i ≤ T i , ∀i.

div.head: IV. PROGRESSION MODEL AND MISMATCH TO UNIPROCESSOR SCHEDULING
div.p: The results in [10]- [12], [14], [15], [17], [19], [21], [24], [30], [34], [35] assume that the schedulability analysis in NoCs is somehow related to a corresponding uniprocessor fixedpriority scheduling problem. However, this has never been formally proven. We note that we do not claim any implication of correctness or incorrectness of existing timing analyses in the literature. We only explain the mismatch, which may be provable under certain assumptions.

In this section, we detail why the link-based arbitration problem does not match the uniprocessor scheduling model and illustrate the subsequent problems in response-time analyses using uniprocessor scheduling theory. To explain the mismatch, we focus on the possible buffer states of one instance (i.e., message) of a flow f i under analysis. Let B i denote the state vector of the number of flits that are buffered in the cores and switches involved in Λ i . Suppose that there are η i links involved in Λ i . Note that the first element in B i denotes the number of flits of f i in the source core left to be sent and the last element in B i denotes the number of flits that have been received at the destination core.

In the following analysis, we assume that the NoC is fully synchronized in time. Therefore, in each time unit, a buffered flit can be forwarded to the next node (a core or a switch). Since the NoC works in discrete time, we can observe the changing of the vector B i over time when considering only the time units at which the message is sent.

When a flit is sent in a time unit at the j-th link in Λ i , then the number of flits of the j-th node is reduced by 1 and the number of flits of the (j + 1)-th node in V i is incremented by 1. For notational brevity, let y j be a vector of η i + 1 elements in which all the elements are 0 except the j-th element that is Fig. 1: Progressions of a message which involves 2 cores and 2 switches, i.e., 3 links, when C i = 10. The numbers associated with an edge indicate the number of buffered flits at the respective switches or cores. The red dashed path illustrates the beginning of the fastest progression and the blue dashed path illustrates the beginning of a slowest progression.

-1 and the (j + 1)-th element that is 1, e.g., y 1 + y 3 implies that the first and the third link transmit one flit in this time unit and the number of flits buffered at the interconnected nodes are incremented and decremented respectively. Definition 1 (Progression). Consider a buffer state B i at time t, in which all elements in B i are non-negative integers. Suppose element z j is either 0 or 1 for j = 1, 2, . . . , η i and at least one of them is 1. Specifically, when z j is 1, the j-th link sends one flit forward. Let Y be ηi j=1 z j y j . For a buffer state B i , z j for j = 1, 2, . . . , η j , and a vector Y , the change of the buffer state is valid if • all elements in B i + Y are non-negative integers that do not exceed the buffer capacities B, and
div.formula: • the j-th element in B i is ≥ z j+1 for j = 1, 2, . . . , η i -1.

div.head: If the change of the buffer state is valid, we say that the flow makes a progression in this time unit.
div.p: In each time unit, a link may or may not be utilized to send a flit of f i in the switching mechanism. Therefore, there are 2 ηi -1 combinations of the vectors of y. Note that progressions do not have to take place in two consecutive time units. If the message is not sent in the next time unit, there is no progression of the message. As an illustrative example, consider C i = 10 and that the message is sent from a core A 1 via V 1 and V 2 to core A 2 . If one flit is sent in a time unit, we get B i = (C i -1, 1, 0, 0). Now, there are three possibilities for the next time unit when the NoC transmits a flit or multiple flits of the message:
div.formula: • B i = (C i -1, 0, 1, 0): In this case, A 1 does not send any flit but R 1 sends a flit to V 2 . The progression is due to Y = (0, -1, 1, 0). • B i = (C i -2, 2, 0, 0): That is, A 1 sends one flit to V 1 but V 1 does not send a flit to V 2 , i.e., Y = (-1, 1, 0, 0). • B i = (C i -2, 1, 1, 0): That is, A 1 sends one flit to V 1 and
div.p: V 1 sends a flit to V 2 , which means that the progression is due to Y = (-1, 1, 0, 0) + (0, -1, 1, 0) = (-1, 0, 1, 0). This example is illustrated in the first three levels of the tree in Fig. 1. In each of the above states, the next progression has to be considered. Due to space limitations, we only illustrate the progressions that are possible when B i is (9, 0, 1, 0). Definition 2 (A Complete Series of Progressions). A complete series of progressions is a sequence of progressions defined in Definition 1, one after another, starting from B i = (C i , 0, 0, . . . , 0) and finishing with B i = (0, 0, . . . , C i ).

A safe analysis of the worst-case response time or the schedulability for sending the message should consider all possible complete series of progressions of f i . If we only account for the number of time units when the message of f i is transmitted, it is not difficult to see that the slowest one only sends one flit forward per progression, in which the switching mechanism results in C i × η i iterations of progressions. Moreover, the fastest one sends one flit (if available) forward for all cores and switches involved in the path λ i per progression, which results in
div.formula: C i + η i -1 iterations of progressions.
div.p: All the results in [10]- [12], [14], [15], [17], [19], [21], [22], [24], [30], [34], [35] assumed that the corresponding uniprocessor scheduling problem can use C i + η i -1 as the worst-case execution time of the corresponding sporadic task to represent the flow f i . This implicitly assumes that the flow f i takes the fastest complete series of progressions. Such uniprocessor analyses are only valid when the other iterations of progressions are accounted for correctly. However, the fastest complete series of progressions for f i may not always be possible. To ensure the correctness of the analysis, some additional time units should be included. Many patches have been provided to account for such additional time units after the series of flaws found in [10], [15], [17], [19], [21], [23], [30], [34].

Informally speaking, the researchers in [10]- [12], [14], [15], [17], [19], [21], [23], [24], [30], [34], [35] have tried to construct their analyses by linking the problem to a corresponding uniprocessor scheduling problem. Most of them were later found to be flawed, e.g., [10], [15], [17], [19], [21], [23], [30], [34], or without a formal proof, e.g., [11], [12], [22], [24]. 2 However, none of them has seriously considered all the possible progressions for transmitting f i . Whether the worst-case response time analysis for preemptive worm-hole switching is equivalent to any specific form of uniprocessor scheduling problem remains an open question.

We strongly believe that the worst-case response time analysis or the schedulability analysis for worm-hole switched fixed-priority network-on-chip is highly complex, since the timing behavior is not uniprocessor equivalent, contrary to the assumptions in the literature. In a uniprocessor system, if a job is executed for δ time units, the execution time of the job is reduced by δ time units. However, sending δ flits can result in different series of progressions in the NoC.

If we want to consider the complete path Λ i as a single shared resource, like in [10]- [12], [17], [19], [21], [22], [24], [30], [34], [35], and analyze the worst-case behavior of the corresponding instance of the uniprocessor scheduling problem, the mapping from the complete series of the progressions to the uniprocessor problem must be proved.

The recent counter examples provided by Xiong et al. [34] are due to backpressures when the buffer space is limited. However, we conjecture that the existing analyses that assume uniprocessor equivalence are not rigorous even when the buffer space is unlimited due to the mismatch explained above. Please note that we do not claim that such a mapping is impossible for dynamic switching protocols, like wormhole switching. However, such mappings are potentially very difficult to achieve due to the large search space. Furthermore, safe approximations and upper bounds are also missing in the literature. In both cases, a correct proof should explain how to safely account for the number of iterations in the progressions of the flows and map them to the corresponding execution time in the constructed instance of the uniprocessor scheduling problem. Therefore, we choose to provide such a mapping for a less flexible dynamic switching protocol.

div.head: A. Problem Definition
div.p: In this paper we consider the interrelated problem of the scheduler design and the corresponding scheduling analysis with respect to real-time constraints.

The scheduler design problem studied in this paper is defined as follows: Given a collection of cores A, switches V, links Λ and a given set F of sporadic flows with real-time constraints on the NoC. How should the switching mechanism (scheduling algorithm) be designed such that:

• the progression model provably matches the execution model of uniprocessors • real-time guarantees can be formally verified • the routing does not have to obey specific deadlock avoidance schemes and can thus be subject to real-time optimizations Analogously, the schedulability test problem studied in this paper is defined as follows: We are given a NoC, defined as a collection of cores A, switches V, and links Λ. For a given set F of sporadic or periodic flows on the NoC and a switching mechanism, the objective is to validate whether the messages (instances of the flows) can meet their deadlines.

We assume that the cores and switches are synchronized perfectly with respect to time, which means that there is no clock drift in the NoC. Otherwise, the clock drift must be considered carefully. One solution is to introduce additional delays and interferences to pessimistically bound the impact due to clock drifts. Moreover, we assume a discrete time, i.e., the NoC operates in the granularity of a fixed time unit and the finest granularity is the flit.

V. SIMULTANEOUS PROGRESSING SWITCHING PROTOCOLS Nikolíc et al. [22], [24] published the most recent result for the worst-case response time analysis. Specifically, the approach in [22] is based on a new concept, which utilizes two network domains, one for arbitration and one for data transmission.

To the best of our knowledge, there is no formal proof to demonstrate the connection between the progressions of the messages on a NoC and the corresponding instance of the uniprocessor scheduling problem. We note that the analytical difficulty is potentially due to the flexibility introduced in the switching mechanism.

In the position papers by Wilhelm et al. [33], Axer et al. [2], and Lee [18] the authors state that system properties that are subject to predictability constraints should already be considered and guaranteed from the design. Lee [18] emphasizes the dual notion of models in engineering. That is, the model of the system is not only used for analysis and subsequent design, but is also the specification of the system behaviour. Since the worm-hole switching protocol was not designed with predictability constraints in mind, designing new protocols that can be safely analyzed without losing too much flexibility or efficiency can be an alternative.

Instead of proving the complex scenarios in the standard worm-hole switching, we propose another protocol which has only one complete series of progressions. These less flexible switching protocols, called SP 2 , achieves timing predictability by enforcing that a flow f i is eligible to transmit on its route if and only if it can be allocated all the links in Λ i inparallel. In other words, the links used by a flow f i either all simultaneously transmit one flit of this flow (if it exists) or none of them transmits any flit of this flow. As a result, for a progression of f i in a time unit, some links in Λ i may be reserved even though there is no flit to be transmitted over this link in this time unit.
In order to formally define the schedules and analyze the schedulability, we introduce the following definition.

div.head: Definition 3 (Schedule).
div.p: A schedule S λj (t) : R → N is a function that maps time t in the continuous domain to the unique flow index that is scheduled on the link λ j at that time. Furthermore, we use S λj (t) = ∞ to denote that λ j is idle at time t.

We use the Iverson bracket to indicate whether a flow f i is scheduled on a link λ j at time t. 3 For convenience, we use S Λj (t) to indicate the ordered set of schedules {S λ k (t) | λ k ∈ Λ j }. Moreover, we abbreviate our notation to a single value, i.e., S Λj (t) = i to denote that all links in Λ j schedule flow f i at time t. Using this notation, we formally define the property of SP 2 as follows. Definition 4. A schedule S implements SP 2 if for all t ≥ 0, for each static routing path Λ i of every flow f i , the following implication holds:
div.formula: [S λ k (t) = i for some λ k ∈ Λ i ] =⇒ [S Λi (t) = i]
div.p: In general, SP 2 can be implemented with any strategy that ensures Definition 4. We will focus on work-conserving priority-based SP 2 scheduling with message-level-fixed priorities. Such strategies can be dynamic-priority algorithms (i.e., two messages of flow f i may have different priorities) and fixed-priority scheduling algorithms (i.e., all messages of flow f i have the same priority).

When two messages intend to use one link at the same time, the higher-priority message is scheduled and the lower-priority message is suspended. Whenever a message is suspended in one of its links, it is suspended in all of its links. We focus on fixed-priority scheduling in the remainder of this paper.

div.head: VI. SP 2 SCHEDULING ANALYSIS
div.p: For a scheduling protocol P , a real-time schedulability analysis of a flow set F validates whether no flow in the flow set misses its deadline under any valid schedule generated by P . Such a validated flow set is hence called feasibly schedulable by P or infeasible otherwise. Furthermore, an analysis of a schedulability test for an algorithm P is called sufficient if all flow sets that are deemed to be feasibly schedulable by this test are actually feasibly schedulable. Likewise the test is called necessary, if every flow set that is schedulable by algorithm P is verified to be feasibly schedulable by the corresponding schedulability test. A necessary and sufficient schedulability test is called exact. In the remainder of this paper, we will derive a sufficient (only) schedulability test.

For each flow under analysis, we identify the higherpriority flows that may cause interference. These flows can be partitioned into a direct contention domain and an indirect contention domain. We define a (direct) contention domain of two flows by identifying the set of higher-priority flows that share at least one link and thus potentially directly interfere with each other. Then, we consider the (indirect) contention domain of the flow under analysis, i.e., flows that do not directly share a link with this flow under analysis but interfere with flows in the (direct) contention domain. In the remainder of this paper, we implicitly assume that the flow set is indexed such that a flow f i has higher priority than a flow f j if i < j.

div.head: A. Buffer and Virtual-Channel Considerations
div.p: The number of buffers and virtual channels within a NoC switch impact the hardware complexity, energy consumption and switching speeds and thus must be considered. By the SP 2 property, each flow only requires a single flit-sized buffer in each switch along its static path in order to be transmitted without any additional blocking time. This is due to the reason that the incoming link of a switch (on a flow's path) is only granted to that flow if and only if the outgoing link is granted to that flow as well as is illustrated in the fastest progression in Fig 1 . Nonetheless, in this naive design, each flow requires a unique virtual channel to transmit without blocking. This comes at a cost since each virtual channel must be arbitrated separately, which requires additional multiplexers and demultiplexers in the switch. Due to space limitations, we only hint to how the reduction to limited virtual channels can be traded off with additional latency in SP 2 and how to revise the schedulability analysis in Section VI-B accordingly.

In any schedule generated by SP 2 (under flit level preemption), a switch requires at most as many virtual channels (of flit sized buffers) as the number of flows that cross that switch. We then design a SP 2 protocol that reserves a channel and buffer slot at each switch in priority order (on transmission request). A flow is eligible to send if the reservation is granted on each switch, which can be achieved since SP 2 is a global scheduling scheme. By doing this, lower-priority flows from the direct contention domain may cause additional interference due to priority-inversion in the same virtual channels.

Due to the fact that in SP 2 this reservation scheme eliminates circular waiting it is thus deadlock-free. Therefore, in SP 2 scheduling for network-on-chips, the path diversity is not constrained to deadlock-free routing schemes like X-Y Routing but can utilize any arbitrary routing scheme. This advantage may offset some of the additional overheads described in this section.

div.head: B. Schedulability Analysis
div.p: In this section, we explain how the schedulability analysis for preemptive fixed-priority Simultaneous Progressing Switching Protocols can be related to the work-conserving fixed-priority preemptive uniprocessor selfsuspension scheduling problem. In real-time scheduling theory, self-suspension denotes the property of an executable entity to be exempted from the scheduling decisions for a specified amount of time, i.e., the self-suspension time. In our analysis, we use self-suspension to model a flow f j that is eligible to be scheduled using any work-conserving algorithm at a given time t due to being the highest-priority flow and being active (released and not yet finished), but is not transmitted due to indirect contention. We prove that this (indirect) contention can be related to self-suspension behaviour in uniprocessor real-time scheduling and thus show the applicability of existing self-suspension aware schedulability analyses. We formally define and prove the self-suspension equivalent property of fixed-priority scheduling using the SP 2 .

We only briefly introduce the uniprocessor self-suspension problem and refer the reader to the existing literature [5], [6] for further information. In short, self-suspension refers to the exemption of a ready schedulable entity from the scheduling decision for a certain amount of time. This exemption behavior is modeled as dynamic self-suspension and multi-segment selfsuspension in the literature. In the former, the suspension pattern can be arbitrary and is only parametrically upper bounded by the total self-suspension time. This flexibility comes at the cost of more pessimism in the timing analyses. In the latter, an upper bound of the duration and the number of a task's suspension intervals is known and can thus be used in the timing analyses. In this paper, we consider the dynamic self-suspension model and the corresponding timing analyses.

Under the fixed-priority SP 2 , each flow has a priority, assumed to be unique in this section. To formalize the direct contention domain of a flow f i under analysis, we denote the set of higher-priority flows of f i that share at least one link as dom(f i ) = {f j ∈ F | j < i , Λ j ∩ Λ i = ∅}. In our analysis here, we assume work-conserving fixed-priority arbitration:

• a flow transmits further if none of its link is used by any higher-priority flow, and • a flow does not transmit further if one of its link is allocated by another higher-priority flow. Note that we analyze the schedulability of each flow individually under the assumption that the schedulability of all higher-priority flows has already been validated. In order to formally quantify the times t such that a flow f j is eligible to transmit on all links in Λ i in-parallel using Simultaneous Progressing Switching Protocols but is not transmitting, i.e., self-suspension behaviour, we give the following definition.
Definition 5 (Λ i -self-suspended). A flow f j is said to be Λ iself-suspended at a time t using a SP 2 protocol, if all the following conditions are satisfied:

1) f j is active at t, i.e., released and not yet finished 2) f j is the highest-priority flow on all the links in Λ i at time t 3) f j is not visible to flow f i , i.e., Λ i Λ j and Λ i ∩Λ j = ∅ 4) f j is not scheduled on all the links, i.e., ∀λ k ∈ Λ i S λ k (t) = j at time t Note that, according to condition 3, we especially require Λ i = Λ j , since the self-suspension behaviour can only occur due to contention that is transparent to the flow under analysis. In the following theorem, we formally bound the set of flows that exhibit self-suspension behaviour in order to safely account for the additional interference.

div.head: VII. DISCRETE-TIME SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS
div.p: In this section, we elaborate on the discrete-time SP 2 response-time analyses. A possible implementation is further detailed in Section VIII. The arbitration in SP 2 is achieved by using two networks, one for arbitration (called the arbitration net) and one for data transmission (called the data net). The arbitration net and data net both operate in the discrete time domain, with a fixed epoch, denoted as Δ. Specifically, we consider the information (state) of both nets to be stable and available at time 0, Δ, 2Δ, . . ., etc. The arbitration (in the arbitration net) of the k-th epoch is responsible for ensuring the all-or-nothing property of the messages to be sent in the data net of the (k + 1)-th epoch. From an analysis perspective, the arbitration net poses a dual response-time analysis problem. That is, the arbitration can be seen as a response-time analysis problem of transmission requests (with release enforcement at epoch intervals) and transmission grants between all competing flows, where the epoch duration is set to the longest response-time among all arbitration messages of flows of interest. Furthermore, transmissions are only granted at epoch intervals. The epoch duration Δ is an artifact from the implementation and not constrained to any specific implementation. In order to analyze the discrete-time response-time of a flow, the transmission time of a flow using SP 2 without any interference must be computed, which is given in the following note.

Note 1 (Transmission-Time). Let C i denote the length of a message in flits and let Δ denote the epoch in integer multiples of a flit. Then, the transmission of a message using a discrete-time SP 2 implementation requires
• Δ time to progress through the static path Λ i from the source to the destination (without any interference).
Using these properties, we can restate our Corollary 1 for the discrete-time case.

div.head: VIII. IMPLEMENTATION SKETCH OF SP 2
div.p: The architectural implementation of the priority-based SP 2 providing the all-or-nothing property requires to rethink pre-vious switch designs. In state-of-the-art worm-hole switching protocols, the decision at each switch is local, whereas the all-or-nothing property requires global decision making.

The SP 2 is a general concept, and thus there could be different possible realizations. In this section, we provide a possible centralized arbitration, achieved by using two networks, one for arbitration (called the arbitration net) and one for data transmission (called the data net). The arbitration net and data net both operate in the discrete time domain, with a fixed epoch, denoted as Δ. Specifically, we consider the information (state) of both nets to be stable and available at time 0, Δ, 2Δ, . . ., etc. We note that the arbitration and response-time analysis can in general also be accomplished by using only one net to send both arbitration and data messages in an interleaving manner. This can be implemented using TDMA with one slot for arbitration and one slot for data transmission. The timing overhead for arbitration is the same as for the implementation here with two nets, and is thus omitted.

The arbitration (in the arbitration net) of the k-th epoch is responsible for ensuring the all-or-nothing property of the messages to be sent in the data net of the (k + 1)-th epoch. We focus on the arbitration net of the k-th epoch and assume that the messages have different priorities. For the simplicity of discussion, we assume that the network starts at time 0.

div.head: A. Centralized-Priority Arbitration
div.p: In centralized-priority arbitration, the set of flows that can communicate in a given epoch is determined by a centralized arbiter. We dedicate one core in the network to the arbitration. Every flow that is admitted to the system is stored in the centralized arbiter, i.e., in a look-up table with a unique flow id (encoding the flow's priority), number of epochs that are required for transmission without any interference, source, destination, and a bit vector path which encodes the flow's static path. Additionally, a ready bit is stored in the lookup table to indicate that the flow is ready, i.e., eligible for arbitration. An integer sent maintains the information of how many epochs have already been sent to reset the ready bit upon transmission completion. The arbitration phase recurs every epoch and is structured as follows. At first, all sources that need to communicate send the flow ids of the flows ready to transmit to the arbiter using either a separate arbitration net or time-division multiplexing in the data net, depending on the network size and tolerable latency. The arbiter waits until it receives all requests during an epoch. Then, all flows that are admitted to transmit in the next epoch are determined by iterating through the look-up table and by verifying if all required links of this flow are available. This is accomplished by a bit-wise AND operation of the currently allocated links encoded in a bit vector and the path bit vector of the flow of interest. Finally, the arbiter sends back the flow id of the flows that can communicate in the next epoch to the source cores. Since all information regarding the flows is known in advance, sources that need to communicate in the (k + 1)-th epoch send their requests for arbitration when the k-th epoch is executed. Thus, the additional latency can be hidden.

div.head: B. Routing of the Arbitration Messages
div.p: Since, the length of an epoch is dependant on the longest transmission latency of the arbitration messages, it is beneficial to minimize this latency. For proposed centralized arbiter, we assume that all the cores are connected in a N×N 2D-Mesh, whilst the arbitration logic is implemented in software in the center core. The source cores in the 2D-Mesh are partitioned into 4 partitions such that each partition sends an arbitration request to the arbiter core simultaneously, which is equipped with 4 read-write ports. Each source core injects packets, thus N 2 -1 requests arrive at the arbiter in total. Under the assumption that an arbitration request can be fully transmitted in each cycle, the number of required cycles is given by (N 2 -1)/4 + 1 = N 2 /4 , where one additional cycle is due to the fact that even the closest core to the arbiter requires at least one hop. Analogously, if an arbitration request requires b cycles to be fully transmitted over a single link, b • N 2 /4 cycles are required for the arbitration communication. We emphasize that the routing in the arbitration net (and the clusters) is done statically to achieve the above property. Especially, we note that the all-or-nothing property does not have to hold for the arbitration net. Fig. 3: Overhead for the arbitration communication in μs for varying number of flows per core (FPC), 2D-Mesh dimensions, and link bandwidths. Note that the communication overhead is independent from the arbiter core frequency.

div.head: C. Centralized-Priority Arbitration Evaluation
div.p: In our experiments, the number of flows with a unique priority on each source core is varied with the total number of cores in the network. Specifically, we assume that each core sends up to a fixed number (denoted as flows per core (FPC), e.g., 1, 2, or 4) of flow ids in one arbitration epoch. Then, we asses the arbitration overhead as well as the communication overhead for different core frequencies and link bandwidths. In these experiments, we implemented the SP 2 arbitration algorithm in software and measured the required time for varying core frequencies. We emphasize that in a real realization the arbitration should be done in hardware. Arbitration Overhead Measurements The arbitration overhead is calculated by measuring the execution time of the arbitration algorithm explained in Section VIII-A. This arbitration algorithm was prototyped in C++ and run on an Intel Xenon Gold 6126 CPU core at 2.6 GHz. Based on these measured execution times and the known core frequency of the measuring system, we calculate the overhead for different core frequencies in the range of 800, 900, . . . , 3000 MHz as shown in Fig. 2. Communication Overhead Measurements The communication overhead is determined by calculating the required number of cycles such that all arbitration requests (from all source cores) are transmitted to the arbiter and the responses are received at the source cores. Each arbitration request requires F •α many bits, where F is the number of flows per core and α is the length of the vector that encodes all priorities. Using the above explanations, it can be seen that ((F +1)•α• N 2 /4 )/β time units are required for the arbitration communication, where β denotes the bandwidth of the links. The results are presented in Fig. 3 for different link bandwidths accordingly. Overhead Results As shown in Fig. 2, the overheads for the communication and arbitration increase with the number of flows per core as well as with the dimension of the 2D-Mesh. For 256 flows (4 FPC) in a 8 × 8 mesh, the communication overhead is 64 μs for 10Mbps, which suggests that the communication overhead for 4×4 and 8×8 2D-Meshes is low enough such that an arbitration within the data plane could be a feasible alternative. The communication overhead for 1024 flows (4 FPC) in a 16 × 16 mesh and 10 Mbps links is 320 μs but can be reduced to 16 μs for 200 Mbps links. The data suggest that the overhead can become too large for higher dimensions and large number of flows. In these cases, other approaches for the arbitration net are required.

div.head: IX. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we discuss the fundamental difficulty of worstcase timing analysis of flit-based pipelined transmissions over multiple links in-parallel in network-on-chips. The space of possible progression states that need to be covered by an analysis hints to the mismatch with uniprocessor scheduling theory and their assumptions, thus making analyses complex and prone to being optimistic. To increase the analyzability, we propose SP 2 , in which the links used by a message either all simultaneously transmit one flit of this message or none of them transmits any flit of this message. For this family of protocols, we formally prove the relation between the uniprocessor self-suspension scheduling problem and the SP 2 scheduling. We also provide a sufficient schedulability analysis for fixed-priority SP 2 scheduling. We note that the existing link-based switching and the proposed SP 2 are in fact two extreme scenarios with respect to the complete series of progressions. The SP 2 approach always results in the fastest complete series of progressions in any case by sacrificing the possibility to send part of the messages even when only one link is blocked by another higher-priority message/flow. The link-based switching mechanism (worm-hole protocol) allows the flexibility to send only one flit of a flow forward at a time unit in the NoC, but it has to potentially consider the slowest complete series of progressions of the flow in the worst case. This paper provides protocols that can be implemented with different strategies.
